The Perils of Broad CAM Definitions in Industrial Leases

In manufacturing and heavy industrial leases, the Common Area Maintenance (CAM) clause is often the most significant driver of unbudgeted operational volatility. Landlords frequently draft these provisions using expansive, "catch-all" language designed to pass through virtually any cost associated with the property's upkeep. For a manufacturing tenant, the danger lies in the lack of distinction between routine, day-to-day maintenance and significant, long-term capital expenditures.

The primary trap involves the inclusion of "capital improvements" within the definition of operating expenses. While a landlord may argue that repaving a heavy-duty access road or upgrading a transformer is a "maintenance" item, such an expense is fundamentally a capital improvement that enhances the long-term value of the asset. Without specific language to the contrary, you may find yourself subsidizing the landlord's long-term property appreciation through your monthly CAM reconciliations. Furthermore, many leases include "gross-up" clauses that allow landlords to charge tenants for services based on a hypothetical 100% occupancy rate, even if the building is significantly under-occupied, artificially inflating your share of the costs.

Strategic Protections for Manufacturing Tenants

To protect your manufacturing margins, your lease must move beyond simple "caps" and focus on rigorous, enforceable "exclusions." An elite-level negotiation focuses on three specific pillars of protection:

  • Capital Expenditure Exclusions: Explicitly exclude any costs related to the replacement, renovation, or structural improvement of the building or common areas, unless such costs are specifically categorized as "repairs" under GAAP standards.
  • Controllable vs.Uncontrollable Caps: Negotiate a fixed percentage cap (e.g., 5%) on "controllable" expenses—such as landscaping, cleaning, and security—while allowing the landlord more flexibility on "uncontrollable" items like property taxes and insurance.
  • Audit Rights and Verification: Ensure the lease grants you the right to audit the landlord's books and records to verify that the CAM charges are being applied accurately and that no excluded capital costs have been surreptitiously included in the operating expense pool.

Manufacturing operations require predictable overhead to maintain competitiveness. Allowing a landlord to unilaterally dictate the scope of "maintenance" is a direct threat to your bottom line. Do not enter a long-term industrial lease without a forensic review of your CAM obligations.
